quotes.text: Though sincerity and confidence have many points of resemblance, they have yet many points of difference. Sincerity is an openness of heart, which shows us what we are, a love of truth, a dislike to deception, a wish to compensate our faults and to lessen them by the merit of confessing them.
quotes.section: Reflections on Various Subjects (1665–1678) › I. On Confidence

quotes.text: Confidence always pleases those who receive it. It is a tribute we pay to their merit, a deposit we commit to their trust, a pledge which gives them a claim upon us, a kind of dependence to which we voluntarily submit. I do not wish from what I have said to depreciate confidence, so necessary to man.
quotes.section: Reflections on Various Subjects (1665–1678) › I. On Confidence

quotes.text: We should make it a rule never to have half confidences. They always embarrass those who give them, and dissatisfy those who receive them. They shed an uncertain light on what we want hidden, increase curiosity, entitling the recipients to know more, giving them leave to consider themselves free to talk of what they have guessed. It is far safer and more honest to tell nothing than to be silent when we have begun to tell.
quotes.section: Reflections on Various Subjects (1665–1678) › I. On Confidence

quotes.text: Satire is at once the most agreeable and most dangerous of mental qualities. It always pleases when it is refined, but we always fear those who use it too much, yet satire should be allowed when unmixed with spite, and when the person satirised can join in the satire. It is unfortunate to have a satirical turn without affecting to be pleased or without loving to jest.
quotes.section: Reflections on Various Subjects (1665–1678) › II. On Difference of Character

quotes.text: Raillery is a kind of mirth which takes possession of the imagination, and shows every object in an absurd light; wit combines more or less softness or harshness.
quotes.section: Reflections on Various Subjects (1665–1678) › II. On Difference of Character

quotes.text: There is a difference between an ardent and a brilliant mind, a fiery spirit travels further and faster, while a brilliant mind is sparkling, attractive, accurate.
quotes.section: Reflections on Various Subjects (1665–1678) › II. On Difference of Character

quotes.text: Though the gifts of the mind are infinite, they can, it seems to me, be thus classified. There are some so beautiful that everyone can see and feel their beauty. There are some lovely, it is true, but which are wearisome. There are some which are lovely, which all the world admire, but without knowing why. There are some so refined and delicate that few are capable even of remarking all their beauties. There are others which, though imperfect, yet are produced with such skill, and sustained and managed with such sense and grace, that they even deserve to be admired.
quotes.section: Reflections on Various Subjects (1665–1678) › II. On Difference of Character

quotes.text: The word taste has different meanings, which it is easy to mistake. There is a difference between the taste which in certain objects has an attraction for us, and the taste that makes us understand and distinguish the qualities we judge by.
quotes.section: Reflections on Various Subjects (1665–1678) › III. On Taste

quotes.text: Some have a species of instinct (the source of which they are ignorant of), and decide all questions that come before them by its aid, and always decide rightly. These follow their taste more than their intelligence, because they do not permit their temper and self-love to prevail over their natural discernment. All they do is in harmony, all is in the same spirit. This harmony makes them decide correctly on matters, and form a correct estimate of their value. But speaking generally there are few who have a taste fixed and independent of that of their friends, they follow example and fashion which generally form the standard of taste.
quotes.section: Reflections on Various Subjects (1665–1678) › III. On Taste

quotes.text: We should never say anything with an air of authority, nor show any superiority of mind. We should avoid far-fetched expressions, expressions hard or forced, and never let the words be grander than the matter.
quotes.section: Reflections on Various Subjects (1665–1678) › V. On Conversation

quotes.text: We are sure to displease when we speak too long and too often of one subject, and when we try to turn the conversation upon subjects that we think more instructive than others, we should enter indifferently upon every subject that is agreeable to others, stopping where they wish, and avoiding all they do not agree with.
quotes.section: Reflections on Various Subjects (1665–1678) › V. On Conversation

quotes.text: We should observe the place, the occasion, the temper in which we find the person who listens to us, for if there is much art in speaking to the purpose, there is no less in knowing when to be silent. There is an eloquent silence which serves to approve or to condemn, there is a silence of discretion and of respect. In a word, there is a tone, an air, a manner, which renders everything in conversation agreeable or disagreeable, refined or vulgar.
quotes.section: Reflections on Various Subjects (1665–1678) › V. On Conversation

quotes.text: All men want to be different, and to be greater than they are; they seek for an air other than their own, and a mind different from what they possess; they take their style and manner at chance. They make experiments upon themselves without considering that what suits one person will not suit everyone, that there is no universal rule for taste or manners, and that there are no good copies.
quotes.section: Reflections on Various Subjects (1665–1678) › VII. On Air and Manner

quotes.text: Few men, nevertheless, can have unison in many matters without being a copy of each other, if each follow his natural turn of mind. But in general a person will not wholly follow it. He loves to imitate. We often imitate the same person without perceiving it, and we neglect our own good qualities for the good qualities of others, which generally do not suit us.
quotes.section: Reflections on Various Subjects (1665–1678) › VII. On Air and Manner

quotes.text: But, yet acquired qualities should always have a certain agreement and a certain union with our own natural qualities, which they imperceptibly extend and increase.
quotes.section: Reflections on Various Subjects (1665–1678) › VII. On Air and Manner

quotes.text: We should not speak of all subjects in one tone and in the same manner. We do not march at the head of a regiment as we walk on a promenade; and we should use the same style in which we should naturally speak of different things in the same way, with the same difference as we should walk, but always naturally, and as is suitable, either at the head of a regiment or on a promenade.=
quotes.section: Reflections on Various Subjects (1665–1678) › VII. On Air and Manner

quotes.text: Thousands of people with good qualities are displeasing; thousands pleasing with far less abilities, and why? Because the first wish to appear to be what they are not, the second are what they appear. Some of the advantages or disadvantages that we have received from nature please in proportion as we know the air, the style, the manner, the sentiments that coincide with our condition and our appearance, and displease in the proportion they are removed from that point.
quotes.section: Reflections on Various Subjects (1665–1678) › VII. On Air and Manner

quotes.text: Our virtues are most frequently but vices in disguise.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: What we term virtues are often but a mass of various actions and diverse interests, which fortune or our own industry manage to arrange; and it is not always from valour or from chastity that men are brave, and women chaste.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Self-love is the greatest of all flatterers.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Passion often renders the most clever man a fool, and even sometimes renders the most foolish man clever.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: The passions are the only advocates which always persuade. They are a natural art, the rules of which are infallible; and the simplest man with passion will be more persuasive than the most eloquent without.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: In the human heart there is a perpetual generation of passions, such that the ruin of one is almost always the foundation of another.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: We all have strength enough to endure the misfortunes of others.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Philosophy triumphs easily over past and future evils; but present evils triumph over it.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: We need greater virtues to sustain good than evil fortune.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Neither the sun nor death can be looked at steadily.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)
quotes.cite: Maxim 26. Sometimes incorrectly translated as "with a steady eye".

quotes.text: The evil that we do does not attract to us so much persecution and hatred as our good qualities.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: If we had no faults, we should not take so much pleasure in noting those of others.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Jealousy lives upon suspicion; and it turns into a fury or ends as soon as it passes from suspicion to certainty.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: We promise according to our hopes; we fulfill according to our fears.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Self-interest speaks all sorts of tongues and plays all sorts of characters, even that of disinterestedness.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Those who apply themselves too much to little things often become incapable of great ones.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: A man will often believe himself a leader when he is led; while with his mind he endeavours to reach one goal, his heart insensibly drags him toward another.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: One is never so happy or so unhappy as one fancies.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: To succeed in the world we do everything we can to appear successful already.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: The happiness and misery of men depend no less on temper than fortune.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Sincerity is an openness of heart; we find it in very few people; what we usually see is only an artful dissimulation to win the confidence of others.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: What grace is to the body, good sense is to the mind.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: It is difficult to define love. In the soul it is a passion to rule; in the mind it is sympathy; and in the body it is only a hidden and tactful desire to possess what we love after many mysteries.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: There is no disguise which can hide love for long where it exists, or simulate it where it does not.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: There are very few people who are not ashamed to be loved when they no longer do.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: If we judge love by the majority of its results, it resembles hatred more than friendship.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: We may find women who have never indulged in an intrigue, but it is rare to find those who have intrigued but once.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: There is only one kind of love, but there are a thousand different versions.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Neither love nor fire can subsist without perpetual motion; both cease to live so soon as they cease to hope, or to fear.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: True love is like the appearance of ghosts: everyone talks about it but few have seen it.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: The love of justice is simply in the majority of men the fear of suffering injustice.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Silence is the surest resolve for him who distrusts himself.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Friendship is only a reciprocal conciliation of interests, and an exchange of good offices; it is a species of commerce out of which self-love always expects to gain something.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: It is more disgraceful to distrust than to be deceived by our friends.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Everyone complains about his memory, and no one complains about his judgment.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Old men delight in giving good advice as a consolation for the fact that they can no longer provide bad examples.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: A man may be ungrateful but is less chargeable with ingratitude than his benefactor.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Everyone speaks well of his heart; no one dares speak well of his mind.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: In the adversity of our best friends we often find something that is not exactly displeasing.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)
quotes.cite: Maxim 99. This maxim is found only in the 1665 edition, and was removed by the author in later editions.

quotes.text: The mind is always the dupe of the heart.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Those who know their minds do not know their hearts.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Nothing is given so profusely as advice.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: There are good marriages, but no delicious ones.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: The intention of cheating no one lays us open to being cheated ourselves.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: We are so used to disguising ourselves from others that we end by disguising ourselves from ourselves.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: If we resist our passions, it is more through their weakness than our strength.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: The truest way to be deceived is to think oneself more knowing than others.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Sometimes one must be base in order not to be tricked by a clever man.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: It is easier to be wise for others than for oneself.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: There are people who would never be in love had they not heard [others] speak of love
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: When not prompted by vanity, we say little.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: We would rather speak ill of ourselves than not talk about ourselves at all.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: The stamp of great minds is to suggest much in few words; by contrast, little minds have the gift of talking a great deal and saying nothing.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Usually we only praise to be praised.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: The refusal of praise is only the wish to be praised twice.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: It is more difficult to avoid being ruled than to rule others.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: One must not just have great qualities, but also economize them
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: The art of using moderate abilities to advantage wins praise, and often acquires more reputation than actual brilliancy.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: It is easier to seem worthy of positions one does not have than of those one does.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: It is better to set one's mind to bearing the misfortunes that are happening than to think of those that may happen.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Our repentance is not so much sorrow for the ill we have done as a fear of the ill that may befall us.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Only great men have great faults.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: The defects and faults in the mind are like wounds in the body. After all imaginable care has been taken to heal them up, still there will be a scar left behind.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: What often prevents us from abandoning ourselves to one vice is that we have several.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: The desire to appear clever often prevents one from being so.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: There are foolish people who recognize their foolishness and use it skillfully.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Who lives without folly is not as wise as he thinks.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: As we age, we become more foolish and wiser.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Most people judge men only by success or by fortune.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Hypocrisy is an homage that vice pays to virtue.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Too great a hurry to be discharged of an obligation is a kind of ingratitude.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Fortunate people seldom mend their ways, for when good luck crowns their misdeeds with success they think it is because they are right.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: It is a great folly to wish to be wise alone.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Nobody deserves to be praised for goodness unless he is strong enough to be bad, for any other goodness is usually merely inertia or lack of will-power.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: It is less dangerous to treat most men badly than to treat them too well.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: There is great skill in knowing how to conceal one's skill.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: True eloquence consists in saying all that need be said and no more.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Some people's faults are becoming to them; others are disgraced by their own good traits.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: In all professions we affect a part and an appearance to seem what we wish to be. Thus the world is merely composed of actors.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: The pleasure of love is in loving; we are happier in the passion we feel than in what we inspire.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Hardly any man is clever enough to know all the evil he does.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Absence extinguishes the minor passions and increases the great ones, as the wind blows out a candle and fans a fire.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: It is impossible to fall back in love with what one has stopped being in love with.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: We always like those who admire us; we do not always like those whom we admire.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: The gratitude of most men is but a secret desire to receive even greater benefits.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: We often forgive those who bore us, but we cannot forgive those whom we bore.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Moderation has been called a virtue to limit the ambition of great men, and to console undistinguished people for their want of fortune and their lack of merit.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: There are many predicaments in life that one must be a bit crazy to escape from.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Lovers never get tired of each other, because they are always talking about themselves.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: The extreme pleasure we take in talking about ourselves should make us afraid that we may scarcely be giving any to our listeners.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: It is not a pain to give to ingrates, but it is an intolerable one to be obliged to a dishonest man.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: In jealousy there is more of self-love than love.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: We confess to little faults only to persuade ourselves we have no great ones.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: We pardon to the extent that we love.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: We hardly find any persons of good sense save those who agree with us.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: What makes us so bitter against people who outwit us is that they think themselves cleverer than we are.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Jealousy is always born with love but does not always die with it.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: There are few honest women who are not tired of what they do.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Mediocre minds usually dismiss anything which reaches beyond their own understanding.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: The greatest fault of a penetrating wit is to go beyond the mark.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: We may bestow advice, but we cannot inspire the conduct.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: There are few people who are more often wrong than those who cannot suffer being wrong.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: What makes the vanity of others insufferable to us is that it wounds our own.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Luck must be dealt with like health: enjoy it when it is good, be patient when it is bad.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: There is a certain dignity of manner independent of fortune, a certain distinctive air which seems to mark us out for great things. It is a value we set upon ourselves without realizing it, and by means of this quality we claim other men’s deference as our due. This does more to set us above them than birth, honors, and merit itself.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: There is merit without attainment, but no attainment without some merit.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: We should often be ashamed of our very best actions if the world only saw the motives which caused them.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: The vivacity which increases with old age is not so far removed from folly.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: In love, the first healed is the best healed.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Nothing prevents us being natural so much as the desire to appear so.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: It is easier to know man in general than to know one man.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: In friendship and in love, one is often happier because of what one does not know than what one knows.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: We try to make virtues out of the faults we have no wish to correct.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Innocence is very far from finding as much protection as crime.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Of all violent passions, the least unbecoming to a woman is love.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: In their first passion, women love their lovers; in all the others, they love love.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Only firm people can be truly soft.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Those who have had great passions are happy all their lives and would be unhappy to have been cured of them.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: Quarrels would not last long if the fault were only on one side.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: It is useless to be young without being beautiful, or beautiful without being young.
quotes.section: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678)

quotes.text: It is a kind of happiness to know how unhappy we must be.
quotes.section: Later Additions to the Maxims

quotes.text: How can we expect others to keep our secrets if we cannot keep them ourselves?
quotes.section: Later Additions to the Maxims

quotes.text: Preserving your health by too strict a diet is a tedious illness.
quotes.section: Later Additions to the Maxims

quotes.text: We should not be upset that others hide the truth from us, when we hide it so often from ourselves.
quotes.section: Later Additions to the Maxims
quotes.cite: Maxim 11 from the Manuscrit de Liancourt.

quotes.text: We are eager to believe that others are flawed because we are eager to believe in what we wish for.
quotes.section: Later Additions to the Maxims
quotes.cite: Maxim 25 from the Manuscrit de Liancourt.

quotes.text: Sometimes it is pleasant for a husband to have a jealous wife: he always hears what he loves being talked about.
quotes.section: Later Additions to the Maxims
quotes.cite: Maxim 48 from the Manuscrit de Liancourt.

quotes.text: It is harder to hide the feelings we have than to feign the ones we do not have.
quotes.section: Later Additions to the Maxims
quotes.cite: Maxim 56 from the posthumously published 1693 edition of the Maximes.

quotes.text: Small minds are hurt by the smallest things
quotes.section: Later Additions to the Maxims

quotes.text: The reason that there are so few good conversationalists is that most people are thinking about what they are going to say and not about what the others are saying.
quotes.section: Later Additions to the Maxims
quotes.cite: Réflexions diverses, IV: De la conversation.

quotes.text: One must listen if one wishes to be listened to.
quotes.section: Later Additions to the Maxims
quotes.cite: Réflexions diverses, IV: De la conversation.

quotes.text: Funeral pomp is more for the vanity of the living than for the honor of the dead.
quotes.section: Later Additions to the Maxims
quotes.cite: "Pensées Tirées des Premières Éditions," Réflexions: Ou, Sentences Et Maximes Morales de La Rochefoucauld (1822)
